turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: Okay so, the model we're gonna take apart today is called Kimi K3, and it has two point eight trillion numbers in it. And right now that number means nothing — it's just a big number. The point of this whole thing is that by the end, it will mean something. You'll know where all of them live, and what each group of them is doing.

turns.speaker: danny
turns.text: Yeah. And the honest pitch for sticking around is — it's so much simpler than that number makes it sound. Not easy. Simple. There's a difference, and it's the good kind.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: So let's start with the job, because the job is the whole thing. You give the model some text. It hands back a probability for every token that could come next. That's it. That's the entire interface.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: Watch the loop. Text goes in. One forward pass through the machine. Out comes a distribution — every possible next token, each with a probability. Pick one. Append it to the text. And go again.

turns.speaker: danny
turns.text: And every single thing you've ever seen a chatbot do... is that loop. There's no database in there, no grammar engine, no lookup table. One function, run over and over, feeding its own output back in.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: Right. So, foundations. I'll assume you know what a vector is — a list of numbers, an arrow in space, same object, two pictures of it.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: The figure on screen adds a third picture — the block. Because at this scale, a vector isn't three numbers, it's seven thousand. The arrow is the intuition. The list is the algebra. The block is the size the algebra actually runs at.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: What I want to slow down on is the dot product. Because the entire model is built out of this one operation. And if it stays fuzzy, everything after it stays fuzzy.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: So. Two vectors. You multiply them component by component... and then you add everything up.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: Take the two on screen. a is four, one. And b is two, three. Four times two... eight. One times three... three. Add them. Eleven.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: That's the dot product — the same eleven the projection panel lands on. Two vectors in... one number out.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: Now. The mechanics are trivial. The real question is what that number means. And the picture to hold onto is... the dot product measures agreement. Same direction? Large, and positive. Perpendicular? Zero. Not small... exactly zero. Opposite? Negative. It's a signed score. It can say these two agree, it can say they're unrelated, and it can say they actively oppose each other.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: And you can see why, from the structure. Multiply and add... means every component pair gets a vote. Both positive? That term votes yes. Signs disagree? Votes no. Bigger components... bigger votes. The sum is the tally. That's all a dot product is. An election, over dimensions.

turns.speaker: danny
turns.text: And here's why that one operation deserves all that airtime — this didn't land for me until embarrassingly late. In this model, everything is a vector. The words are vectors. The meaning of a word is a vector. So the question, does this word relate to that word — the machine can't ask it in English. It asks it as a dot product. Every time. That's the only question this thing knows how to ask.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: That's exactly where this is going. And when you hear matrix multiply — look at the figure. It's just dot products arranged in a grid. Each row of the matrix dots against the vector, independently, all at once. The same election, run thousands of times in parallel. The reason GPUs matter, the reason the hardware industry looks the way it does — it's that this one operation got fast.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: Okay. Next piece — the neuron. Which sounds biological, and it isn't. It's about four symbols of algebra.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: A neuron takes its inputs... dots them against a set of weights it owns — same operation again, notice — and then does one more thing. It bends the result. And the standard bend is almost insulting. Negative? Becomes zero. Positive? Left alone. That's it. That's the famous nonlinearity.

turns.speaker: danny
turns.text: Okay, hang on though — because this is where I want you to slow down. That bend looks like nothing. It's a clamp. Why does everyone treat it like it's load-bearing?

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: Because without it... depth is fake. Watch what the figure does — it deletes the bend. If every layer is just a matrix multiply, then two layers is a matrix multiply of a matrix multiply. And that composes... into one matrix. Same for three layers. Same for a thousand. Any stack of purely linear layers collapses into a single one. You could train a thousand-layer network... and I could replace it, exactly, with one matrix.

turns.speaker: danny
turns.text: A thousand layers... and it can't do anything one layer couldn't.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: Nothing. But the bend breaks the collapse. And once it's broken, there's a classical result — it's on screen — that a network with enough bent neurons can approximate essentially any function. Two of them make a bump. Scaled bumps tile any curve you like. That's from the eighties, by the way. Representation was never the problem. The problem was finding the right weights, and doing it fast enough to matter.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: One footnote for honesty — production models use a smoother cousin of that clamp. Same idea, gentler corner. The difference lives entirely in the slope, which matters because the slope is what training rides on. Which is the next thing.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: So — learning. And I want to de-mystify two words right away, because they made me close the tab the first time I met them. Loss... and gradient.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: The loss is one number. It measures how badly the model just did. That's the entire concept. And the gradient is the direction, in weight-space, that makes that number smaller. One number down... one direction downhill.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: The machinery that finds the direction is the chain rule from calculus, made mechanical. The forward pass computes — and caches what it saw. The backward pass starts at the loss and walks the graph in reverse, multiplying one local derivative per edge. By the time it reaches a weight, buried a dozen layers deep, the product of all those local slopes tells you exactly — if I nudge this weight, here's what happens to the loss.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: So the whole recipe is on screen. Forward, and cache. Measure the loss. Backward for the gradients. Take a small step downhill. And then... do it again.

turns.speaker: danny
turns.text: See, this is the part I had to sit with. Nobody designs the model. You just... keep rolling downhill, a few million steps, and the design falls out. The hill does the designing.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: One practical note that matters at scale: you don't compute the loss over all your data before each step — you grab a small batch, get a noisy estimate of the gradient, and step anyway. The figure shows the two paths. Same start, roughly the same destination... a sixth of the arithmetic. Noise turns out to be a price worth paying for speed. Hold that thought, because at trillion scale it becomes the only option.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: Okay. Two more pieces and the objective is complete. The model's last layer spits out a raw score for every token in the vocabulary — a hundred and sixty thousand of them. They're called logits, and they're ugly. Some are negative. They don't add up to anything. They're not probabilities yet.

turns.speaker: danny
turns.text: So you clean them up.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: You clean them up, and that's softmax. Watch the steps. Exponentiate every score — that's e to the score, which is just a smooth way of making everything positive that never quite hits zero. Then divide each one by the total. Now they're all positive... and they sum to one. That's a probability distribution. Terrifying name. Two moves.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: And then cross entropy scores the prediction. The curve on screen is the whole story — it's minus the log of the probability you gave the right answer. Certain and correct? You pay nothing. Hedged? You pay a little. Confident and wrong? The penalty grows without bound. It's a surprise meter.

turns.speaker: danny
turns.text: Which means the thing this model is minimizing — for months, across thousands of machines — is its own surprise. That's it. That's the objective. Everything else in this video is machinery for doing that one thing at scale.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: So here's a fair question. Predict-the-next-word is not a new idea. People had language models in the nineties. Why did this take until twenty seventeen?

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: Well — the first idea is counting. Count how often each word follows each phrase. And the figure shows why it dies: every extra word of context multiplies your table by the size of the vocabulary. A hundred and sixty thousand. Past three or four words, the table has more cells than the corpus has words... so almost every count is exactly zero. You haven't seen most four-word phrases. Neither has the internet.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: So the second idea — recurrent networks. Read one word at a time, left to right, carrying a running summary. And this actually works... but look what the summary is. A fixed-size vector that has to hold everything so far. The whole book... squeezed through a straw.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: And there's a quieter killer. Training signals travel backwards through every step. Each step multiplies the signal by roughly the same factor. If that factor is slightly less than one... after a hundred steps the signal is basically gone. Slightly more than one... it explodes. Learning across long distances just... doesn't happen.

turns.speaker: danny
turns.text: But that's not even the reason they lost. This is the part that reframed the whole story for me. If word five can't start until word four is done, then a thousand chips can't help you — they'd just be standing in line. The wall wasn't intelligence. It was parallelism. The breakthrough everybody calls attention is really — a model you could run all at once.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: Okay, so before any of that machinery — text has to become numbers. And the way it happens is more interesting than it sounds.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: You could feed the model characters — but then every word is a long sequence and the model spends its capacity learning to spell. You could feed it whole words — but there are infinitely many, and one typo is a word it's never seen. So you land in between.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: The algorithm is almost embarrassingly greedy. Start with raw bytes. Find the pair that occurs most often... glue it into one unit. Repeat, a hundred and sixty thousand times. Common words fuse into single tokens. Rare words stay in pieces. The vocabulary is literally a compression dictionary, learned from the data.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: And then each token gets its vector by lookup. A table with a hundred and sixty thousand rows, one per token, each row seven thousand numbers long. Do the arithmetic — that table alone is over a billion parameters. Our first billion, accounted for. And here's the part I love: those rows are learned. Nobody assigns them.

turns.speaker: danny
turns.text: And they end up organized. Words that mean similar things end up pointing in similar directions — nobody asked for that. It just... helped prediction, so the hill rolled there.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: Now we can build the thing. And the picture that makes the whole architecture make sense is called the residual stream.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: There's a stream of vectors running straight down the model, top to bottom — one lane per token. Every layer reads from the stream... computes something... and adds its result back in. Adds. Not replaces.

turns.speaker: danny
turns.text: Okay and why is that one word doing so much work? Adding instead of replacing?

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: Remember the recurrent networks — the signal shrinking a little at every step until it was gone? Addition fixes that. When layers add, there's an unbroken path from the loss all the way down to layer one — the gradient can flow along the stream untouched. That one design choice is why ninety layers is trainable and a ninety-layer chain is not.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: And inside, each layer has exactly two jobs, alternating. Attention — that's communication. Tokens talk to each other. Then the feed-forward block — that's computation. Every token thinks by itself, no talking. Communicate... compute. Communicate... compute. Ninety times.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: And the atom under all of it is the same one from the start of this video — a matrix of learned weights, multiplying a vector. Training means nudging those entries. Inference means streaming them past a multiplier. There is no other ingredient.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: The figure on screen draws one layer with areas proportional to parameters. Take a second with it, because it kills the most common misconception in this whole subject.

turns.speaker: danny
turns.text: Yeah — this genuinely surprised me. Everyone talks about attention like it's the whole model. Look at the areas. Most of the parameters are in the feed-forward blocks. The boring part. Attention is the clever part... it is not the big part.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: One bit of housekeeping and we can open the layer up. Numbers flowing through ninety layers of multiplies want to explode or vanish — so before each sublayer, you rescale the vector to a standard size. That's normalization. The figure shows the two places people have put it — inside the stream, or beside it. Beside won. Everything trains smoother when the stream itself stays untouched.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: And here's a fact I find genuinely satisfying: the modern block is the twenty-seventeen block... edited mostly by deletion. Every removal validated the same way. Take it out. Watch the loss curve not move. Keep it out.

turns.speaker: danny
turns.text: Nine years of architecture research, and the diagram's mostly the same picture with pieces missing. The rhythm — attention, feed-forward, add, add — hasn't moved since twenty seventeen.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: Alright. Attention itself. And I want to start with the problem, not the mechanism. Take the word — it — in a sentence. On its own, that token means nothing. To understand it, you have to go find what it's pointing at. Every token has this problem. Meaning is spread across the sentence, and each position needs a way to go... collect it.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: So here's the mechanism. Every token manufactures three vectors from its own embedding — by three learned matrix multiplies, same atom as always. A query... what am I looking for. A key... what do I contain. And a value... what I'll hand over if you pick me.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: Then every query gets dotted against every key. And you know exactly what that means now — it's the agreement election. Each pair of tokens gets a score... how relevant is that one, to me.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: Softmax the scores — now each token holds a set of mixing weights that sum to one. And then it takes a weighted blend of everyone's values. That's it. That's attention. Each token went shopping, and came back with a basket.

turns.speaker: danny
turns.text: And the reason this beat the recurrent networks — it's not that it's smarter. Look at the figure. The whole thing — every query against every key, every blend — is a couple of matrix multiplies. Every token, every pair... at once. No waiting for word four to finish. You can throw a thousand chips at it. That's the parallelism wall, gone.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: And the figure on screen is small enough to check by hand, which I'd genuinely encourage. The learned part is just the three projection matrices. Everything after — scores, softmax, blend — is fixed arithmetic. Attention has surprisingly few parameters. It's mostly... choreography.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: Two details that matter. First — you divide the scores by the square root of the dimension before the softmax. Because dot products over thousands of coordinates come out huge, the softmax saturates into a one-hot spike... and the gradients die. One divide fixes it.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: Second — the mask. Position five must not see position six. Otherwise, predicting token six is easy... it already read it. Training would be a take-home exam with the answer key stapled to the back.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: Run several of these in parallel — different projections, same mechanism — and the heads specialize. One tracks syntax. One tracks what pronouns refer to. Nobody assigns those jobs. They emerge, because dividing the labor helped prediction.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: One catch, and it's a real one. Attention treats the sentence as a set. Reorder the words... and nothing changes. Word order — the thing language is made of — is invisible to it.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: The fix is on screen, and it's geometric. Rotate each query and key by an angle proportional to its position — like clock hands, fast dials and slow dials. Now the dot product between two tokens depends on how far apart they are. Order rides in on the geometry itself. Nothing extra to store.

turns.speaker: danny
turns.text: And then look at this last figure — ten years of attention variants. And almost every one of them has the same motive. Not smarter attention... smaller memory. Shrink what each token leaves behind. Hold that thought, because it's about to become the whole story.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: Because here's the bill. Every token attends to every other token. Double the context... quadruple the work. And K3 runs context out to a million tokens.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: At that length there are two separate enemies, and the figure puts them on one axis. The score matrix — that's the quadratic one, it murders training. And the cache of keys and values every past token leaves behind — that one grows linearly, but it's what generation has to hold in memory... forever.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: The first fix is pure engineering, and it's beautiful. Never build the big matrix at all. Cut it into tiles... stream each tile through the fast memory next to the arithmetic units... and merge the softmax across tiles with a running trick. Exact same answer. A fraction of the memory traffic. That's FlashAttention, and the answer doesn't change — only the electricity bill.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: The second fix is architectural. Instead of storing every token's full keys and values... store a compressed summary, and decompress on the fly. The byte anatomy is on screen. That's MLA — and it's one of the two attention systems K3 actually ships.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: The other one is more radical. Drop the softmax entirely... and attention collapses into a running memory you update as you read — constant space, no matter how long the context. Pure versions of this blur — everything smears together. So you gate it... teach it to forget on purpose... and correct old memories instead of piling on top. That family ends at KDA, which is the linear half of K3.

turns.speaker: danny
turns.text: And K3's answer to which one is right is — both. Look at the interleave. Three linear layers, then one exact one. Three cheap... one careful. The exact layers keep recall sharp, the linear ones keep the memory flat. Honestly my favorite kind of engineering — no winner, just a ratio.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: With two honest footnotes on screen about what million-token context really means. Softmax has to sum to one, so surplus attention parks on the earliest tokens... and models genuinely lose things in the middle of long documents. Claimed context and usable context are not the same number.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: Now — the trick that makes two point eight trillion affordable at all. Mixture of experts.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: Here's the dilemma. Most parameters live in the feed-forward blocks, and bigger blocks genuinely know more. But in a dense model, every parameter runs for every token. Capacity and compute are chained together — you can't grow one without paying for the other.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: So you break the chain. Replace the one big block with eight hundred and ninety-six small ones — experts. A tiny learned router looks at each token and picks a handful. The rest... don't run at all.

turns.speaker: danny
turns.text: This is my favorite fact in the whole model. Two point eight trillion parameters... and per token, under two percent of them wake up. The rest are just... asleep. You get the knowledge of the enormous model at the running cost of a fifty-billion one.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: There's one genuine danger, and the figure animates it. The router is trained by the same downhill process as everything else... which creates a feedback loop. An expert that gets lucky early attracts more traffic... which trains it more... which attracts more traffic. Left alone, a few experts absorb everything and the rest atrophy into dead weight. So you add pressure toward balance — K3's version watches the traffic distribution and nudges the router whenever any expert hogs it.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: And at this point... the arithmetic closes. Embeddings, attention, eight hundred ninety-six experts per layer, sixty-one layers. Add it all up — two point eight trillion, no leftover mystery. Every parameter now has an address.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: So that's the machine. Empty. Where does the knowledge come from?

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: It starts with a scrape of the public web... and then you throw almost all of it away. Watch the cascade. Deduplicate. Filter for language. Score for quality. Strip the boilerplate. What survives is a few percent of what you started with.

turns.speaker: danny
turns.text: And zoom out on what's left. About fifteen trillion tokens — forty-some terabytes of text. That's the entire diet. Which is not the number anybody puts in a press release... the curation is the moat, honestly.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: Then the loop you already know, run at civilization scale. Grab a batch. Forward pass. Measure the surprise. Backward pass. Nudge every weight. That's it — the same four beats, repeated for months.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: One elegance worth pausing on. A chunk of nine tokens isn't one training example... it's eight. Every prefix predicts its next token, and the mask from the attention chapter means you score them all in a single pass. Nothing about the objective is hand-labeled. The text is its own answer key.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: And here's your first calibrated number. Before training, the model guesses uniformly over a hundred and sixty thousand tokens — cross entropy says that costs log of a hundred sixty thousand... about twelve. Weeks later the loss sits near two. Twelve is ignorance. Two is... most of English, most of code, most of the shape of the world. The entire multi-million-dollar run is that one number, walking down.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: The engineering underneath is its own discipline — no single machine holds this model, so you cut it every way at once. Split the batch. Split the layers. Split the individual matrices. Split the experts. Thousands of chips, all of which have to keep talking to each other constantly, for months, without one of them corrupting the run.

turns.speaker: danny
turns.text: And the loss curve is honestly a little anticlimactic. It falls off a cliff in the first hour... and then it just... crawls. For weeks. That crawl is what the money buys. The last five percent of that curve is where most of the capability lives.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: With one measurement keeping everyone honest — a slice of data the model never trains on. As long as surprise keeps falling on text it's never seen... it's learning the language, not memorizing the file. The day those curves part company, you stop.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: And what comes out the other end of those months is... not a chatbot. This surprises everyone. It's called a base model, and the best description I know is — an internet simulator.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: It doesn't answer questions. It continues documents. Hand it any prefix, and it gives you the distribution over what the internet would plausibly say next. Ask it a question... and it might write you five more questions. Because that's what a page of questions looks like.

turns.speaker: danny
turns.text: And the compression number here is wild. Forty-four terabytes of filtered text... squeezed into five point six terabytes of weights. Call it eight to one. It cannot have memorized the internet — there's no room. It was forced to learn the patterns instead of the pages. The compression is the intelligence. Same phenomenon as the embeddings organizing themselves, just... at civilization scale.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: And here's the strangest gift of scale. Put three worked examples in the prompt... and the model picks up the pattern and does a fourth. Nothing was trained. The weights are frozen — they were frozen before your prompt existed. Somewhere in learning to continue any document... it learned to spot and extend patterns on the fly. Nobody engineered that. It was discovered, not designed.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: And once you see it, the chatbot trick is obvious. Write a transcript where one speaker is a helpful assistant... and let the simulator continue it. An assistant, conjured out of a document format. That's genuinely how it started. Everything in the next section is just making that trick... reliable.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: So — post-training. Turning the simulator into something you'd actually hand to a person. The budget here is a rounding error next to pretraining... and it's where the product gets made.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: Step one is supervised fine-tuning, and mechanically it's nothing new — same next-token loss, but the data is now conversations, many written by paid contractors demonstrating what good help looks like. One detail worth seeing on screen: the chat format is just tokens. Turns, roles, the whole interface... it's a document convention the model learns. And the loss only counts the assistant's tokens — you grade the model on its lines, not the user's.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: That teaches the format and the manner. But imitation has a hard ceiling — the model can't get better than the demonstrations. And demonstrations can't cover judgment... which of two decent answers is better.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: So the next stage optimizes against preference and against checkable results. K3's flavor is on screen. Take one prompt. Sample a group of sixteen attempts. Score each one — and where possible, score with a verifier. Run the code. Check the arithmetic. A verifier can't be flattered. Then each attempt is trained against its own group's average. Above your siblings... reinforced. Below... suppressed.

turns.speaker: danny
turns.text: The textbook analogy here actually holds up. Pretraining is reading the book. Fine-tuning is copying the worked examples. And this stage is... doing the practice problems at the back. And it's the only stage of the three that can exceed its teacher, because the answer key isn't a human performance — it's whether the thing actually ran.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: And then something happens that nobody fully expected. You train on math and code with verified rewards... and the answers start getting longer. On their own. Length was never rewarded. The model just finds that working through steps... checking them... backing up when one fails... wins more. Watch the curve — accuracy climbing, and answer length climbing next to it, unasked.

turns.speaker: danny
turns.text: It starts checking its own work. Nobody wrote a rule that said do that. Now — how much of that is genuinely new reasoning, versus surfacing what pretraining already put in there... is actively argued about, and worth being honest that it's argued about.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: The axis that decides everything is on screen now, and if you remember one thing from this section, make it this. When the reward is checkable — code that runs, arithmetic that's right — you can push optimization as hard as you like. The reward can't be conned. But when the reward is a learned model of what people prefer... it's a stand-in. And stand-ins can be gamed.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: The failure even has a name — reward hacking. Watch the sequence: the score keeps climbing... and then you read the top-scoring output. Confident tone. Elaborate structure. Empty content. It found what the grader falls for, and the grader isn't reality. So you patch the reward... and another seam opens. That arms race is a big part of what alignment work actually is, day to day.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: Okay. Actually running the thing. And there's an asymmetry here that explains the way every chatbot feels.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: Two phases. First, prefill — your whole prompt goes through in one parallel pass. That's the attention trick again, all tokens at once... it's fast. Then decode — writing the reply. And each new token has to wait for the one before it. There's no way around the wait... the loop is the machine.

turns.speaker: danny
turns.text: So that's why it streams at you word by word. That's not a loading animation. That's the actual computation, arriving as it happens.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: The thing that makes decode affordable at all is the cache. Every past token's keys and values, kept in memory, so each new token only computes itself. And the figure shows the price at scale — with naive attention at a million tokens, that cache would run to nearly two terabytes... per conversation. Now every variant from the attention chapter — the compression, the linear layers, the interleave — snaps into place. That entire zoo exists to shrink this one buffer.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: Last piece of the pipeline — changing a trained model's behavior without retraining it. And the arc on screen ends somewhere absurd, so let's walk it.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: Full fine-tuning moves all the weights — at this scale, that's a data center. LoRA freezes the model, and trains two skinny matrices alongside each big one... under one percent of the parameters, most of the benefit. Squeeze harder — shrink those matrices until, at the far end of the figure... thirteen numbers. Thirteen trained parameters, steering a model of trillions... and on a math benchmark, that recovers most of what full fine-tuning gets you.

turns.speaker: danny
turns.text: Thirteen! Out of trillions. And the fine print is the interesting part — that only works with the practice-problem style training, the reinforcement kind. Try it with imitation and it needs orders of magnitude more capacity. Which tells you the capability was already in there... those thirteen numbers aren't teaching it math. They're flipping a switch that was already wired.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: And it isn't only text anymore. Which sounds like a whole second architecture... and the punchline of this chapter is that it's barely an addendum.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: Because look at what a transformer layer actually consumes. Not text. Vectors. The tokenizer was always an adapter — a text-shaped funnel into a machine that only ever saw lists of numbers. So the question for images isn't... how do we redesign the model. It's just — how do we get pixels into vectors.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: And the answer on screen: cut the image into a grid of little patches. Flatten each patch. Project it to the model's dimension with — one more learned matrix. A patch is a token. That's a vision transformer, and it's the same machine you already understand.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: Audio? Turn the waveform into a spectrogram — sound as an image — and in it goes, a few dozen vectors per second. Video is images times time, with some aggressive merging so the token bill doesn't explode. Same funnel... different spouts.

turns.speaker: danny
turns.text: That's the part that stuck with me. There's no separate image module bolted on the side. Attention never finds out where the vectors came from. One mechanism... every sense.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: So. Two point eight trillion numbers. Embeddings you can count. Attention you can check by hand. Experts you can add up. Where does it go from here?

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: The timeline on screen is nine years — from the paper that started this to a fine-tune that fits in twenty-six bytes. And look at the pattern in it. The core thesis never moved — predict the next token, communicate then compute, add don't replace. Every improvement was an edit at the edges of a frozen center. Attention got cheaper... the linear interleave. Compute got sparser... the experts and their router. Rewards got harder to fool... verifiers instead of preferences. Adaptation collapsed... to thirteen numbers.

turns.speaker: danny
turns.text: Which tells you where the next round comes from, doesn't it? Every open frontier we met tonight is still open. Usable context versus claimed context. Verifiable rewards for things that aren't math or code — that one's enormous. And whether the reasoning is real or retrieved... someone has to actually settle that.

turns.speaker: charlie
turns.text: And whoever settles it will do it with the pieces you now own. Because that was the deal at the start — that the number would mean something. Two point eight trillion numbers. A dot product, a bend, a hill... run at civilization scale.

turns.speaker: danny
turns.text: And now you know what every one of them is for.
